name: Finland
description: Finland offers expats a high quality of life, exceptional safety, and a strong emphasis on work-life balance, making it a highly desirable destination. Its stunning natural environment and efficient public services contribute to a peaceful and well-organized lifestyle.
longdescription: Expat life in Finland is characterized by a strong sense of community, a high standard of living, and proximity to nature, even within urban areas. Finns value personal space, honesty, and reliability, which can initially be perceived as introverted but leads to deep, lasting friendships once established. The country consistently ranks as one of the happiest globally, driven by its robust social support systems, excellent healthcare, and free education. While English proficiency is high, particularly in major cities, learning Finnish is crucial for deeper social integration and expanding career opportunities, as the job market, currently recovering from a recession, can be competitive. The economy is gradually improving after a contraction in late 2023 and 2024, with modest GDP growth expected in 2025 and 2026, supported by declining interest rates and public investment. Finland's society prioritizes equality and sustainability, offering a clean environment and a stable political landscape. Adapting to the long, dark winters is a common challenge, but the thriving cafe culture and appreciation for outdoor activities provide balance.

visas.name: Finland Student Residence Permit
visas.description: Finland's student residence permit for non-EU/EEA nationals enrolled in a full-time degree programme at a Finnish university or university of applied sciences.
benefits: Study at Finnish universities (often tuition-free for EU students)

visas.name: Finland Family Reunification Permit
visas.description: Finland's family reunification permit allows the spouses, registered partners, and minor children of Finnish residents or citizens to join them in Finland, provided the sponsor can support the family financially.

visas.name: Finland Specialist Work Permit
visas.description: Finland's specialist work permit for non-EU/EEA nationals who have been offered a specialist or expert role by a Finnish employer, allowing long-term residence and employment in Finland.
benefits: Work in Finland's thriving tech economy

Citizenship by Descent.desc: A child acquires Finnish citizenship automatically at birth if their mother is a Finnish citizen, or if their father is a Finnish citizen and married to the child's mother. Citizenship is also granted if the child was born in Finland and paternity by a Finnish citizen father was established on or after June 1, 2003, or if maternity by a Finnish citizen (who is not the birth mother) was established on or after April 1, 2019. Citizenship can also be obtained by declaration for a child born abroad out of wedlock to a Finnish parent, an adopted child (12-17 years old) by Finnish citizens, or a young person (18-22 years old) who has lived in Finland for a sufficient period (e.g., 10 years if born abroad, 6 years if born in Finland).

Naturalization.desc: Effective October 1, 2024, the general period of continuous residence required for naturalization has been extended from five to eight years. Only time lived in Finland under a residence permit will be counted. Exceptions to the 8-year rule include: a 5-year residence period for applicants who meet language proficiency requirements, children aged 15 or over, spouses of Finnish citizens, and stateless persons (extended from 4 years). Nordic citizens and spouses of persons working at Finnish missions abroad retain a 2-year residence requirement. Government proposals for a citizenship test and stricter integration/livelihood requirements will be submitted to Parliament in autumn 2024 and spring 2025. During the required residence period, applicants may stay abroad for a total of one year, with no more than three months in the year preceding naturalization.

Birthright.desc: Finnish citizenship is automatically acquired by a child born in Finland if their mother is a Finnish citizen, or if their father is a Finnish citizen and married to the child's mother. Additionally, a child born in Finland acquires citizenship if their paternity by a Finnish citizen father has been confirmed on or after June 1, 2003, or if their maternity by a Finnish citizen (who is not the childbearing mother) has been confirmed on or after April 1, 2019.

Spouse and Family.desc: As of October 1, 2024, the residence requirement for spouses of Finnish citizens seeking naturalization has been extended from four to five years. This applies to spouses of Finnish citizens who have lived together for at least three years, provided they also meet language skills requirements. For spouses of persons working at Finnish missions abroad, the residence requirement remains two years.

tax_advice:
- **Corporate Tax:** Finland levies a flat corporate income tax rate of 20%.
- **Personal Income Tax:** Finland operates a dual income tax system. Earned income is progressively taxed at combined national and municipal rates reaching approximately 56.5%, while capital income is taxed at a flat 30-34%.
- **VAT (Value Added Tax):** The standard VAT rate in Finland increased from 24% to 25.5% on September 1, 2024. A reduced VAT rate of 13.5% (down from 14%) is proposed to apply from January 1, 2026, for items like food, catering, transport, accommodation, and cultural activities.
- **Expatriate Tax Regime (Key Employee Tax):** Eligible international professionals can apply to be taxed at a flat rate on salary. This rate was 32% but is expected to be reduced to 25% for employment commencing on or after January 1, 2026. The regime can apply for up to 84 months (seven years). Finnish nationals returning to Finland may also be eligible for a reduced benefit period of 60 months, subject to a five-year lookback for unlimited tax liability.
local_tips:
- **Cost of Living:** Finland is among Europe's pricier destinations. A single person can expect monthly costs around €1,600-€1,733, and a family of four around €4,787, including rent. Helsinki and Espoo are the most expensive cities.
- **Language:** While many Finns, especially in major cities like Helsinki, speak excellent English, learning Finnish (or Swedish) is highly recommended for job opportunities, social integration, and accessing public services. Finnish is considered a difficult language to learn, with an estimated 1,100 hours needed for professional working proficiency.
- **Safety:** Finland consistently ranks as one of the safest countries globally, with low crime rates. Standard precautions, such as avoiding unlit areas at night and being aware of your belongings in crowded tourist spots, are still advisable.
- **Registration:** Non-EU/EEA citizens staying longer than 90 days require a residence permit. EU citizens must register their right of residence and place of residence if staying over 90 days. Foreigners residing in Finland for over a year are legally required to register in the Population Information System and obtain a personal identity number (henkilötunnus), which is essential for daily life.
- **Climate:** Be prepared for long, dark, and cold winters. Investing in warm clothing and considering light therapy can help with seasonal adjustment.
- **Social Integration:** Finns value personal space and are not prone to small talk. Building friendships may take time, but they tend to be deep and lasting. Actively seeking out social groups and embracing local culture, such as sauna, can aid integration.
